title: The Dreamers: Verne and Tsiolkovsky
summary: A French writer named Jules Verne wrote an exciting story about people fired to the Moon from a giant cannon, and kids all over the world loved it. One of those kids was a Russian boy who had lost most of his hearing, taught himself science from library books, and became a village schoolteacher. He worked out, with pencil and paper, that rockets, not cannons, could carry people into space.

sections.heading: A Gun Club Aims at the Moon
paragraphs: In 1865, a French author named Jules Verne published a novel called De la Terre à la Lune, which means 'From the Earth to the Moon'. Verne was 37 years old and already well known for adventure stories packed with real science, maps and numbers. Readers loved the way he made impossible journeys sound almost possible. This time, he aimed higher than ever: at the Moon itself.

The story begins in Baltimore, in the United States, just after the American Civil War. A group of retired weapons makers called the Baltimore Gun Club is bored, because the war is over and nobody needs their giant cannons any more. Their president, Impey Barbicane, makes an astonishing proposal: they will build the biggest cannon the world has ever seen and fire a shot all the way to the Moon.

The club raises money from people and governments around the world. They choose a site in Florida, a hill near Tampa that Verne calls Stone's Hill, because it is far enough south that the Moon passes almost straight overhead there. There they cast an enormous cannon straight down into the ground, a vertical iron tube about 270 metres (900 feet) long, and they name it the Columbiad. To watch the shot, they even build a giant telescope on a mountain in the Rocky Mountains.

Then the plan changes. A bold French adventurer named Michel Ardan arrives and announces that he wants to ride inside the projectile. Barbicane's bitter rival, Captain Nicholl, an expert in armour plate, had been about to fight a duel with him, but Ardan talks them both into joining him instead. The cannon ball becomes a hollow, cone-topped capsule with padded walls, windows, supplies and, rather charmingly, two dogs. On launch day, huge crowds gather, the Columbiad fires with a gigantic roar, and the three men shoot off into the sky. The book ends with the capsule seen through the telescope, circling the Moon, and the reader left wondering what happens next. Verne answered that in a sequel, 'Around the Moon', published in 1870, in which the travellers loop around the Moon and fall back to Earth, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean.

What made the book special was not just the adventure. Verne tried hard to get the numbers right. He worked with his cousin, a mathematics teacher, to estimate how fast the capsule would need to go to escape the Earth's gravity. The figure in the book, 12,000 yards per second, is about 11 kilometres per second, remarkably close to the real escape velocity of about 11.2 kilometres per second. For a novel written more than 90 years before the first satellite, that is impressive.

Some details also look eerily like the real Apollo missions a century later: a crew of three, a launch from Florida, a giant machine named Columbiad when Apollo 11's command module was named Columbia, a trip around the Moon and a splashdown in the Pacific. In July 1969, as Apollo 11 headed home, Neil Armstrong mentioned in a television broadcast from space that Jules Verne had written a book about a voyage to the Moon about a hundred years earlier. Some of these matches are coincidences, and some come from the simple fact that Florida really is a good place to launch from, but they show how carefully Verne thought things through.

sections.heading: Why a Cannon Would Squash You Flat
paragraphs: There was one huge problem with Verne's plan, and the science fans who read his book soon spotted it. A cannon gives its push all at once. The shot goes from standing still to full speed in the tiny moment it takes to travel up the barrel. To reach about 11 kilometres per second inside a barrel 270 metres long, Verne's capsule would have had to speed up at roughly 22,000 times the strength of normal gravity. Engineers say this as 22,000 g.

What does that mean for a person? When you stand still, you feel 1 g, your normal weight. On a big roller coaster you might feel 3 or 4 g for a moment, which pushes you hard into your seat. Fighter pilots in special suits can handle about 9 g for a few seconds before they risk blacking out. In 1954, an American air force doctor named John Paul Stapp rode a rocket sled that stopped so suddenly he felt about 46 g, but only for a split second, and even that was so painful that he compared the feeling in his eyes to having a tooth pulled without any painkiller. At 22,000 g, a passenger would weigh, for a moment, about as much as dozens of heavy trucks piled on top of them. Nobody could survive that. Verne's travellers would have been squashed flat at the bottom of the capsule.

Could you fix this by making the cannon longer? A longer barrel gives the shot more time to speed up gently. But the numbers quickly get silly. To keep the push down to a bearable 3 g, the barrel would need to be around 2,000 kilometres long, nearly three times the length of Florida from top to bottom. And there is a second problem: air. A capsule leaving the barrel at 11 kilometres per second at ground level would slam into the thick lower atmosphere at a speed where the air in front of it would heat up ferociously and slow it down hard. Even huge guns could not do the job.

People did try giant guns later, but only for small, sturdy, uncrewed shells. In the 1960s, a research project called HARP fired instrument-carrying shells from modified naval guns in Barbados and the United States, and one shot, fired in Arizona in 1966, went up to about 180 kilometres high. That reached space, but the shells were tough little packages that could survive thousands of g. A human, or even most delicate electronics, would not.

A rocket solves this beautifully. Instead of one giant kick, it pushes steadily, for minutes, all the way up. It starts slowly, then speeds up as it burns off fuel and gets lighter, climbing above the thickest air before it goes really fast. The huge Saturn V rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon kept the push on its crews to around 4 g at most, and the Space Shuttle was designed to keep it to about 3 g. Astronauts still feel heavy during launch, but it is uncomfortable, not deadly. In other words: a cannon throws you, a rocket carries you.

Verne could not have known all of this in 1865. But by asking the question so vividly, he got young readers thinking about it. Three of the most important rocket pioneers of the next century, the Russian Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, the American Robert Goddard and the German-speaking Hermann Oberth, all read Verne as youngsters. The first of them was only a small boy when the novel came out, but a few years later he would find it, and it would stay with him for the rest of his life.

sections.heading: The Boy Who Could Not Hear
paragraphs: Konstantin Eduardovich Tsiolkovsky was born on 17 September 1857 in the village of Izhevskoye, in the Ryazan region southeast of Moscow, in the Russian Empire. His father, Eduard, was a Polish-born forester who worked for the government, and his mother, Maria, came from a family of Russian and Tatar background. The family was big and not well off, and they moved several times as Eduard changed jobs.

When Konstantin was about nine or ten, he caught scarlet fever, a dangerous illness that was common in children before modern antibiotics. He survived, but the fever damaged his ears and left him very hard of hearing for the rest of his life. Today, a child with hearing loss can get hearing aids, special teachers and sign language. In the 1860s, in a small Russian town, there was little help of that kind. Konstantin found it almost impossible to follow lessons in a classroom, and other children teased him. He later recalled that his deafness made him feel cut off from people, and that it pushed him to turn inward, to his own thoughts and his own projects.

Then, when he was about 13, his mother died. It was a terribly hard time. Yet the lonely boy did not give up. He read every book he could find at home, especially on mathematics and science, and he loved to build things: little carts, toy windmills, model ships and little machines. His father noticed that his son had a real gift for invention and decided he should have a chance to learn more.

sections.heading: Three Years in a Moscow Library
paragraphs: In 1873, when he was 16, Konstantin travelled to Moscow, then Russia's second city, to study on his own. He could not enrol at a university, partly because of his deafness and partly because he had very little formal schooling. So he made the city's libraries his university. Day after day, he went to the Chertkov Public Library, a free library with a large collection, and read through books on physics, chemistry, astronomy, mathematics and mechanics.

His father sent him a small amount of money each month, but it was barely enough. Tsiolkovsky later remembered spending most of it on books, test tubes, chemicals and materials for experiments, and living mainly on black bread and water. He was thin and shabby, his trousers sometimes stained by acids from his experiments, and the local boys laughed at him. But in the library he found an unusual friend. One of the librarians was Nikolai Fyodorov, a strange and brilliant thinker who believed that science should one day let humanity spread out across the universe. Fyodorov helped the shy teenager choose books and guided his reading. Historians still discuss how much Fyodorov's grand ideas about humanity's future in space shaped Tsiolkovsky's later thinking.

It was during this period, or soon after, that Tsiolkovsky read Jules Verne. The idea of travelling beyond the Earth gripped him. According to a later account, by the age of about 17 he was already thinking about how a real machine could carry people into space. He tried out ideas with whatever he had: he imagined a spinning device to create artificial weight, and he puzzled over how a machine could move in empty space with nothing to push against.

After about three years, in 1876, his father called him home. Konstantin was 19, worn out and underfed, but he had given himself an extraordinary education. He continued studying at home and tutored local students. In 1879 he passed the exam to become a teacher, and in 1880 he was given a job teaching arithmetic and geometry at a school in Borovsk, a small town about 100 kilometres southwest of Moscow. That same year he married Varvara Sokolova, the daughter of the family he lodged with. They would have several children together, and the family's life was often hard and marked by sadness, including the loss of several of their children.

sections.heading: The Schoolteacher of Kaluga
paragraphs: Tsiolkovsky taught in Borovsk for about 12 years, from 1880 to 1892. His students remembered him as kind and enthusiastic, a teacher who showed them experiments and models instead of only making them copy from books. Because of his poor hearing, he sometimes used a home-made ear trumpet, a horn-shaped tube that funnelled sound into his ear.

In his spare hours, he wrote and experimented without stopping. In 1883 he wrote a work called 'Free Space', in which he described what life would be like in a place without weight: how objects would float, how people would move around, and how a craft could be steered by shooting out jets of gas. That last idea is exactly how small thrusters steer spacecraft today. He was only 26.

In 1892, Tsiolkovsky moved with his family to Kaluga, a larger town on the Oka River, about 160 kilometres southwest of Moscow. He would live there for the rest of his life, more than 40 years, teaching mathematics and physics at local schools. His wooden house became his workshop, laboratory and study, with models hanging from the ceiling and papers piled everywhere. Today that house is a museum, and Kaluga is also home to a big museum of space history named after him.

In Kaluga, Tsiolkovsky worked on many inventions, not only rockets. He was fascinated by airships and designed a large airship with a thin metal skin, which he hoped could carry many passengers. Around 1897, he built what is often described as one of the first wind tunnels in Russia, a box through which air could be blown past models so he could measure the forces on them. He also wrote science fiction stories to help ordinary people imagine life in space, including 'On the Moon' and 'Dreams of Earth and Sky', both from the 1890s.

In one of his writings from 1895, inspired by the newly built Eiffel Tower in Paris, he imagined a tower reaching all the way up to space, so tall that at its top objects would float. This 'space tower' is an early version of what people today call a space elevator. Nobody knows how to build one yet, but scientists still discuss the idea.

Much of the scientific world ignored him. He was a provincial schoolteacher, not a professor; he published many of his works himself, with his own small salary; and some of the experts he wrote to did not take him seriously. But he kept going, filling notebook after notebook with ideas.

sections.heading: The Article That Started Space Science
paragraphs: By the late 1890s, Tsiolkovsky had become convinced that the rocket, not the cannon or the balloon, was the only machine that could ever leave the Earth. A rocket carries its own fuel and its own oxygen, so it does not need air. It pushes against its own exhaust, so it can keep speeding up in empty space. And it pushes gently over a long time, so a crew inside could survive.

Around 1897, he worked out a simple but powerful formula describing how fast a rocket can go. In May 1903, he published his ideas in a Russian magazine called Nauchnoye Obozreniye, meaning 'Scientific Review'. The article's title is usually translated as 'Exploration of Outer Space by Means of Reaction Devices', or sometimes 'Exploration of World Spaces with Reaction Machines'. A reaction device simply means a machine that moves by pushing something out of its back, just as Newton's third law describes.

The formula is now called the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, and it is still used by every space agency in the world. You do not need the mathematics to understand its big message. It says two things decide how much speed a rocket can gain. The first is how fast the exhaust gas shoots out of the back: the faster the exhaust, the more speed the rocket gets from every kilogram of fuel. The second is how much of the rocket is fuel compared with the weight of the empty rocket: the more fuel you carry compared with everything else, the faster you can go when it has all burned.

This sounds simple, but it holds a hard lesson. The speed you gain does not grow in a straight line as you add fuel. Each extra tonne of fuel also has to lift itself, so you get less and less extra speed for every tonne you add. To reach orbit, which needs a speed of roughly 8 kilometres per second, most of a rocket has to be fuel. Tsiolkovsky realised that the gunpowder of old war rockets was far too weak for this. He needed something much more powerful.

His answer was liquid fuel. He suggested burning liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen, which together produce very fast exhaust; the reaction makes mainly water vapour. In 1903 nobody could easily make, store or pump these super-cold liquids, so it was a bold idea. But he was right: hydrogen and oxygen later powered the upper stages of the Saturn V that went to the Moon and the main engines of the Space Shuttle.

That same year, in December 1903, the Wright brothers made the first powered aeroplane flight in North Carolina, staying in the air for 12 seconds. So in the very year humans first flew a powered aeroplane a few metres above a sandy beach, a deaf schoolteacher in a small Russian town had already published the science of flying into space. At the time, hardly anyone noticed. The magazine had few readers, and the article had little impact outside Russia for many years. A second part came out in 1911 in a Russian aviation journal, with more following in 1914, and his work gradually found readers among young Russian engineers.

sections.heading: Rocket Trains and the Cradle of Humanity
paragraphs: Over the next three decades, Tsiolkovsky kept adding astonishing ideas. He knew that one single rocket would struggle to reach orbit, because it had to carry all its heavy empty tanks and engines all the way up. So he proposed what he called 'rocket trains', in a book published in 1929. His idea was to join several rockets together and let each one fire in turn, dropping away when its fuel ran out so the others did not have to carry its dead weight. This is the multi-stage rocket, the same idea Siemienowicz had drawn in 1650, but now backed by real calculations. Almost every rocket that reaches orbit today uses stages.

He imagined space stations orbiting the Earth, where people would live and work for long periods. He thought about airlocks, little rooms with two doors, so astronauts could go outside without letting all the air escape. He described spacesuits for working outside a spacecraft. He suggested growing plants in space greenhouses to make food and fresh oxygen, and using sunlight for power. He even described engines that could swivel to steer a rocket, much like the gimballed engines used today. In 1926 he wrote a step-by-step plan for how humanity might gradually move out into space, starting with rocket planes and ending with whole settlements around the Sun.

Life became easier for him only late in life. After the Russian Revolution of 1917, the new Soviet government took an interest in his work. Around 1920 he was granted a pension, which allowed him to stop teaching and concentrate on writing. In the 1920s and early 1930s, young Soviet rocket enthusiasts discovered his books, and he became famous in his own country, treated as a wise old pioneer. Over his life he wrote hundreds of papers, books and stories. Among the young readers he inspired were future Soviet rocket designers such as Sergei Korolev and Valentin Glushko, whose story comes later in this Deep Dive.

Tsiolkovsky never built a real rocket himself. He had no money, no laboratory and no team. His power was in his thinking, and in the way he wrote about space so that others wanted to go there. His most famous line comes from 1911 and is usually quoted in English as: 'Earth is the cradle of humanity, but one cannot live in the cradle forever.' In the Russian original he actually wrote about a planet being the cradle of the mind, or reason, but the meaning is the same. A cradle is where a baby starts life, safe and protected. But babies grow up and, one day, they leave the cradle. Tsiolkovsky believed that humanity would one day grow up and leave the Earth too.

Konstantin Tsiolkovsky died in Kaluga on 19 September 1935, two days after his 78th birthday, and was given a state funeral. He did not live to see any of his dreams come true. But just 22 years later, in October 1957, the Soviet Union launched the first artificial satellite, in the same year that marked the 100th anniversary of his birth. A large crater on the far side of the Moon now bears his name. Many people call him the father of astronautics, the science of spaceflight.

Tsiolkovsky had worked out much of the theory, but he had never fired a liquid-fuel rocket. Someone would have to actually build one, and make it fly. The first person to do that was on the other side of the world. In the autumn of 1899, in Worcester, Massachusetts, a thin and often sickly American teenager climbed a cherry tree in his back yard to trim its branches, looked up at the sky, and found himself dreaming of a machine that could fly all the way to Mars.

deepDive: The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation is usually written as delta-v = v_e × ln(m0 / mf). Here delta-v is the change in the rocket's speed, v_e is the exhaust velocity, m0 is the starting mass with all the propellant on board, mf is the final mass when the propellant is used up, and ln is the natural logarithm. The logarithm is the cruel part. If the exhaust velocity is 4.4 km/s, close to the best hydrogen–oxygen engines, and you want a delta-v of about 9.4 km/s, roughly what reaching low Earth orbit costs once you include losses to gravity and air drag, then m0/mf must be about e to the power 2.14, roughly 8.5. So about 88 percent of the rocket's starting mass has to be propellant, and the tanks, engines, structure and payload must fit in the remaining 12 percent. With kerosene and oxygen, whose exhaust is slower at roughly 3 km/s, the ratio climbs above 20 for a single stage, which is nearly impossible to build. This is why Tsiolkovsky's 'rocket trains', or stages, matter so much: throwing away empty tanks resets the equation partway up. Historians note that the equation was not entirely unique to Tsiolkovsky. A British mathematician, William Moore, had derived a related equation for rocket motion in 1813, and Robert Goddard and Hermann Oberth later reached similar results independently, partly because Tsiolkovsky's work was little known abroad. Tsiolkovsky's distinction is that he was the first to apply it systematically to spaceflight and to draw the big conclusions: liquid propellants, multiple stages, orbital stations. There is also discussion about how his work became so well known. Soviet authorities in the 1930s and later promoted him as a national hero, which helped preserve his papers but also sometimes exaggerated his priority over foreign pioneers. On Verne's cannon, the physics is simple: required acceleration equals v² divided by twice the barrel length. For 11 km/s in 270 m, that is about 220,000 m/s², or roughly 22,000 g. Space guns remain interesting only for very tough cargo, never for people.
funFact: Tsiolkovsky published his key rocket article in 1903, the same year the Wright brothers made the first powered aeroplane flight, so the science of spaceflight was written down before anyone had flown a powered aeroplane.
